utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to raise a couple of matters before hearing the witness. One has to do with the motion filed by the accused, entitled the verification of alleged victim survivals. We have already issued one order for an expedite the response from the Prosecution, I think, by tomorrow. But even before that, the Chamber is of the view that without prejudice to its final determination of the merits of the motion, we would want to hear, Mr. Alarid, next week, and to have as witnesses -- tell me if this needs to be in private session, Mr. Groome. You're an expert in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- the Court gave me till this afternoon to make submissions whether it should be private. And I was going to suggest that the litigation be private but the decision be public for reasons that can spell out before or after Your Honour talks about these matters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we can be in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if Your Honour allow me, I will tell you what we have done so far, why I think it's appropriate that it be handled in private session. But I'm happy to do that afterwards. I was going to suggest that the Chamber that the litigation, the arguments, and the submissions be confidential but that the Chamber's decision be public. I can spell out the reasons if the Chamber wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is it part of the decision that I'm giving which I want to give before hearing from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will just briefly say that there is lot of information in the filing that I'm not sure if the Chamber is going to discuss now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm not discussing the thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I don't know how to do that. And the reason being is this, is I went to this women and knocked on her door and I know exactly where she lives. We entertained the issue, but I did not ambush with her that the full ramifications of, I think, that the revelation of her being alive and her children being alive and her father-in-law having been alive create. I did not forewarn her of the possibility of being drug to court on short order, possibly by subpoena, possibly by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking of subpoenaing her. I just want to you have her as a witness. Because, in any event I would imagine that would you call them as witnesses to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, and I just don't -- I think is insensitive. I felt for them in -- in the way I sort of ambushed them just but knocking on the their. And you know that was --who is this man? And so I'm just sensitive to them. And that's why -- I'd like some advice from the Court, maybe even the other side in terms of -- or Victims Witness Section as well for how to treat this with the utmost delicacy given the nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Our instruction to you would be to get them witnesses here at the earliest opportunity next week. Because in the Chamber's view it would help us in looking at the other matters that are raised in the -- in the motion. And any help that you need, I would instruct the Victims and Witness Unit, through the Registrar, to provide that assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would prefer to treat them as intermediaries as well and that, so I appreciate that. Sometimes you don't know where you can turn on those kinds of issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you must leave no stone unturned. And let us know by Friday how you're getting on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just maybe in light of that, Your Honour, I sent out an e-mail to my experts saying that I'd love to schedule them through the end of the month, and I don't -- I know some of them are objected to. We haven't had time to file responses to those objections, but I would think in a Tribunal scenario the qualifications of the experts tend to fall inside the judge's purview of examining them and the relevance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, I thought we had issued an order on that. Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have issued an order than, which should be out later today, and we have granted the application for them to -- to testify. But, of course, the actual admission of their -- of the statements would be done during the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would expect the Prosecution to have fair opportunity to voir dire the witnesses as to qualifications and foundation with regard to their opinions. So thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just, Ms. Sartorio, you should be near the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Approximately five minutes maybe thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do want to address the Chamber. The Chamber gave me till the prior -- to the start of the evidence to address it on the whether these filings should be public or confidential. As I said yesterday one of the people who as listed as a newly found survivor -- sorry, Your Honour, can I ask that we go into private session before I comprise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any type of written statement to Danny or to anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever shown any documentation with regard to what you would be testifying about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no documentation in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times have you met with persons from the Defence before coming here to testify -- before coming to The Hague to testify? Just that one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back there, in Visegrad, only once. And once or twice we met here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived, right? This time, when I came here to testify, that's when you met with him. It wasn't on another occasion that you met with them in The Hague. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not. Here in The Hague at the hotel, yes, I met up with him once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now did you know there was an indictment out against Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was on TV, back where I live. They showed his arrest on television. They showed these things where I live on the main prime time news bulletin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the allegations were that he was a member of the White Eagles paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know, if you recall, what the allegations were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The news item was about his arrest in Argentina. That's what they broadcast on the news. It was very short. Everybody could see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, I have to ask you have you ever been convicted of a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't convicted for inflicting bodily injury on another person for which you paid a fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would object as to relevance, Your Honour. Only crimes of -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: -- convictions of felonies and crimes involving dishonesty are admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is in the United States, not here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever been convicted for inflicting bodily injury on another person, for which you paid a fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did pay a fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But when I just -- when I asked a minute ago about whether you had any convictions, you didn't believe this was a conviction? I am just curious as to why you said no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought you meant whether I had ever been in custody or in prison, which I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to admit the judgement and this conviction in evidence if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we would object and object specifically because there is a difference in the Serbian language between crime and misdemeanour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Their Honours can read the judgement in English, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think it makes any deference now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's Document 06464891.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it would make a difference as to how it was translated to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, how was it translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That becomes a question to the witness as to his understanding, Your Honour. I don't want to influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you ask him, Ms. Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm is it not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Have you ever been convicted of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's bring it up on the screen. Maybe that is the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: 06464891, please. If you could go to the second page, which ... please. So that both parties can read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in looking at the English translation of this judgement it appears that you were charged with violating a code of an article of the Republika Srpska Criminal Code. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I violated it? It's all different where we are, these trials and everything. If you have connections, it is all a different matter. There was the sister of that person and -- I mean, want to go to trial. I didn't want to pay for a lawyer, but if I had taken a lawyer I would have gotten off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind that. Never mind that. Just answer the question, and let us move on. I think too much time is being spent on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour, I would just like to admit in evidence, and it will speak for it anti-inflammatory and Defence can argue what it wants. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P251 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever been to the village of Mala Gostilja? And I may be pronouncing it wrong. Mala Gostilja never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did pass through before the war. I don't know what you mean when you ask this question. You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. Not once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... know anyone by the name of Miljo [phoen] Joksimovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Mile Joksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's the taxi driver I know, he lives in Visegrad. He doesn't hail from Gostilja; he never lived in Gostilja. He lives in town. Before the war he was a taxi driver, and then they caught him. I don't know that he ever lived in Gostilja because I went to school in Gostilja for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether he lived in Gostilja. First I asked you whether you had been there, and now you're telling -- first you said you passed through before the war, and now you're telling us that you went to school there. So you have spent some time that village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mala Gostilja is a bit further away, and the school is on the other end, closer to Donja Dubovo. I went to school for that four years without ever actually going to Mala Gostilja. It was the first four years of elementary school, and there was a shop newly opened at the very entrance to the village of Mala Gostilja. I don't know how far it stretches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now put that village aside. Now I'm asking you -- I'm going to ask you if you know some people. And the first person was Mile Joksimovic, and you said he was a taxi driver until they caught him. What did you mean until they caught him? Caught him what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I would object to that line of questioning, as being outside the scope of direct examination. Otherwise what is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes to the credibility of the witness. If you would answer my questions, we can get to the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please answer, and let's move on quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript said that you caught him. Is that not what you said? Somebody -- that they caught him. Is that what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This must be an interpreter's mistake, because that's what the witness seemed to have said. He now says I never said that; I don't know who caught him. Maybe you're talking about a different Mile Joksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he still a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He used to drive a bus after the war and in Banja, I don't know if he is retired or not. He has a very peculiar house, with some horns on it, and everybody knows that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by the name of Nedjo Joksimovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Nedjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how well do you know Nedjo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He used to work with my late father, in the forestry business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about Ratko Joksimovic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Ratko too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mojsic, do you know Borisav Mojsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him. He is a neighbour of mine, at the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last person, it's Ljubisa Simjanovic [phoen]. Have you heard of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean Milica Simjanovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ljubi ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. [Previous translation continues] ... were you ever involved in any type of criminal activities with these named individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that information has been provided to the ICTY that you were involved in raiding a village and moving people into a house and burning them alive; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, this is it beyond the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute please. Ms. Sartorio, you have to bring this to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what is basis for these accusations against this witness? We have been provided no information with regards to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm just asking if he is aware of that, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, this is a longer witness, Your Honour. It's quite involved. I have about another half for him in direct. I think I can try and move it along and cut out some questions here and there, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we in private session? Could I request private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do it. Should I read? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may begin, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Dan Ivetic, and it is my privilege and honour to be the one to ask you to answer some questions for us today, and first I want to apologise for not being to that in the same language with you today. I hope you will not take offence at it. And with the assistance of the court usher as soon as she is available, I would like first to present with you a pseudonym sheet that we have prepared for you. Thank you. Now, sir, once this sheet arrives at you -- near you, I would like you to review the document and check the same to make sure that the information contained therein as to your name in full is correct. And then at that point I would ask to you confirm whether it is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Should I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no, you shouldn't read it. You should just read it to yourself and please verify whether the information contained therein as to your full name is accurate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you then to initial the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would ask for it to be introduced under seal as the next available 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D127 [realtime transcript read in error "D127"] under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it should be 1D17; is that accurate or is it 117?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript is incorrect. 1D127.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll have to advise you at the beginning of your testimony that this Chamber has granted protective measures of pseudonym for you so that your full name will not be publicised; however, your voice and image will be publicised only in the public portions of those proceedings. Are you aware of that, and are you willing and able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, we can proceed. But I -- my eye-sight isn't so good anymore. Whenever I don't understand a question, I will ask to you repeat and that's how we can go about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could first go into private session to deal with the biographical background on this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: (redacted) Could you please tell what you say family name predominates in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Do you want me to mention both the Muslim names and the Serbian names?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from that village, sir. Surnames, I'm sorry, surnames.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Well, first the Gavrilovic, Grujic, Milosavljevic, Vasic, Simic, and Bozic. Those are the Serbian last family names and Jasika also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the Muslim surnames?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Kurspahic and Memisevic, Janovic, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We -- if you could please slow down a little bit. I know from talking to you, you like to speak faster, but the transcript is having a hard time keeping up with you, and presume the translation is as well. If you cooperate we can try and get through this better. Now, did you have occasion prior to the war to interact with and know any of the Kurspahics, the Kurspahic family, from the village of Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I always cooperated with them. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: (redacted) And I went to their -- or rather they came to me, and I did all sorts of things for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- okay. And with respect to the Kurspahics, we'll get into that in more detail later as to the relationship with specific members of that family. Right now could you tell us approximately how long have you known various members of the Kurspahic family, the Kurspahic Muslim family from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: (redacted) and there was a craftsman from who I learned I was an apprentice there. And I know all the males by name, but I don't know all the women. But I -- I must have met all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now after the war, do you know if any of the Kurspahics had occasion to either return to Koritnik or visit Koritnik,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Until June they never went anywhere from that village but then about 30 people came --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... might have been mistranslated to you. I'm talking about after the war after the war. I'm talking about after the war, do you know if any of the Kurspahics had occasion to return to Koritnik or visit Koritnik, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes. Three hours houses were built, and they come there and they live there, and they work the land, and they get paid for that. And -- and they have some 30 or 40 beehives, one of the Kurspahics and -- so they have bees, and they worked the land, and they also come to harvest the plums which they sell in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again I would just ask to you focus on my questions and speak slowly so that we make sure we get all this evidence in. I fear some of it is being lost from what I'm seeing on the transcript and what I'm hearing, but I'll deal with that later. Now, sir, with respect to these Kurspahics that have returned to Koritnik for one reason or another, could you tell us the names, the first names of these families that have been back, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Asim returned; Sherif also; Meso, that's what he is called, although his true name is Osman; then Becar's sons, Rade, but they also come over the weekend. Sherif and Asim lived there all the time. Asim died three years ago. His sons come from Sarajevo. Mirza and one, another one, is a Sarajevo police commander. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now do you still have occasion to see and interact with any members of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to interact with members of the Kurspahic family clan that have returned to Koritnik for one reason or another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I spoke to Osman who is called Meso. We meet each other all the time. I spoke to Mirza, he also came to my home. He had coffee with me and juice. Asim also, I spoke to brother Jusa. And I spoke to everybody who came there. And I also spoke to Dzemaja's [phoen] sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just waiting for the translation and transcript to catch up with us. There is something about something you did last year with them, and I see that is not in the transcript. Could you repeat for us what referenced to last year and to Dzemaja's sons whose names you do not know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I bought hay from them. And they have a field there and we -- we bought some hay from them, me and some other Serb neighbours of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And how would you describe the interactions with members of the Kurspahic family today; that is to say, are they friendly towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we are in open session, so I would ask that you be very careful not to mention anything that would reveal your name and identity or place of residence. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you tell us, please, with respect to the time-period before the outbreak of the war, what were relations like between Muslims and Serbs in your locale your region of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Well, not only in my locale but throughout the municipality of Visegrad, I know that relationships were very fine. People visited each other to celebrations, birthdays, and sending off their sons to the Yugoslav army. Everybody invited each other to their homes, and there was no -- no difference was made depending on ethnic background until 1992 when we were surprised by their demeanour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the outbreak of the hostilities in Visegrad, the war, did there come a time when you, yourself, were mobilised into any of the structures, defence structures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes. Such time came on the 10th of April. I was mobilised, but I was a village guard. All of us from the neighbourhood, Muslims, posted sentries in their places, and we in our -- and from 10th to the 19th of April, we were guarding our villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to your mobilisation, what about after that? Were you mobilised or assigned after that to any other duties or any other position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: On the 19th of April, we were mobilised into proper army, and we were stationed in the elementary school at Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And upon being mobilised into the army, did you receive a uniform and/or any other equipment upon your mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Then we wore civilian clothes. We had not received any uniforms, whoever could find some clothes wore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about armaments? When you were part of the village guard and later when you were mobilised into the proper army? What sort of weapons were given to you first, going into each period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: While we were village guards we had no weapons. Whoever had permits to hold hunting weapons, they would use them. After when we went to Prelovo, we were issued with M48, very old gun. Then semi-automatic and some received automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, and moving on. With respect to your military service, did you receive any official documentation at the conclusion of the war relative to your military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I didn't receive any documents. What do you mean? What kind of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is to say, did you receive credit with respect to your pension for the time-period when you served in the official armed forces during the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I did my service from 19th of April, 1992, until the 1st of June, 1993. After that, I had under what duty, at the lines until 1995, 30th of November, 1995. After that, I no longer performed any duties under work duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I have to ask you a very blunt question that may seem odd to you, but since allegations are made in this courtroom every day, I have to ask you this question; and have to apologise in advance and hope you won't be offended by it, by me asking it. But, sir, you were you ever a member of a paramilitary or criminal organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Upon being mobilised and upon being stationed at the Prelovo school, what types of tasks or assignments were you and the other persons that were with you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Well, we were sentries around the village, in the forests in all the villages. I don't want to list all of them. We were guards until the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you have any knowledge of during this -- during the time-period between 1992 and 1995, did you have any knowledge of Milan Lukic, that is to say, what organisation Milan Lukic was a part of, specifically in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I knew Milan Lukic. I knew his parents. I used to see him while my children attended school at Prelovo from grade 4 to grade 8. He was slightly younger than my children. I knew him. I don't know that he belonged to any organisation. He came back from Switzerland via Belgrade in May. I used to bump into his father in the marketplace. There were civilians sleeping next to military tents because they were afraid of spending nights in their villages so they would -- for safety reasons come to sleep in their own tents, next to military tents where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm waiting for the transcript to catch with us. We'll get to all that in a bit. I would again ask you to speak slower so as to minimise the amount of questions that I have to ask as follow up to correct things that are not coming up in the transcript. First of all, do you have any knowledge of what -- of any -- of -- of -- of -- of what structure Milan Lukic was mobilised into in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: When he came in May to Visegrad whenever I used to see him, when I would come to town, I would -- used to see him with a Commander Tomic in the company of Zeljko Tasic and Andric in a Gulf Passat. He would drive, and the commander, Tomic, would be in the passenger seat. It was a red Passat in mint condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now these other people, Commander Tomic, Zeljko Tasic, Vidoje Andric, what structure did they belong to in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Those months, they escorted Commander Tomic. He was the commander, and they were his escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear with respect --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when the counsel repeats back the question to the witness and adds additional information without pointing to it right now, without -- I'd just like to call the attention of the Chamber that it that appears that sometimes the witness gives a certain part of a name, for example, and counsel, when he follows up on that, adds in names or corrects names. I would just like to call the Chamber's attention to that and to request counsel to refrain from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness give the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He has, Your Honour. If you listen to the tape, you will see that he said those names. I cannot be held responsible for the fact that persons who do not speak B/C/S cannot hear the names and do not appear in the transcript immediately. I have to ask the questions and I cannot pay attention to the transcript to see what is coming into the transcript and what is not. I have to listen to the witness, and again I stand by everything that I've asked. And if the tape needs to be reviewed, so be it. I would like to have the tape reviewed for every day of this trial because I seen some things that need to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to -- and now I've lost my train of thought as to where we were going. With respect to this individual you've identify as Commander Tomic, what was he commander of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Police commander. His father was a commander and before that he worked in the offices and his father died. He was appointed as police commander. I know it as a fact, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to those occasions when you would see Milan Lukic and these individuals, where -- where -- where -- where was that? You may have already answered it. I apologise. It is off my screen now. But where would you see them, in what areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: In town or whenever I went to town, they would be there, and this is how I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic now. There's been a lot in this trial about mention about the White Eagles. What about the White Eagles? Did you ever see or hear of Milan being associated with, being either a member or a founder or a leader of the White Eagles group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, never. Milan was never a member of "Beli Orlovi," White Eagles. They came in April, and there were headquarters in the new hotel close to the bridge in Visegrad. They were an army unto themselves. They never mixed with either police or regular military and this is what I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of reputation did the White Eagles have in Visegrad town in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't understand what you meant or what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did they act, and how did they act --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: What they wore you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how did the residents regard them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Serbs and Muslims who knew that they had arrived didn't like it. I don't know any of them. I didn't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say, "I didn't know where they came from," were the persons who called themselves the White Eagles locals or persons who come from outside Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. No local was among them. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was there talk around town or who was reputed to be the leader of this group, the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know who that was. I don't know any leaders or any commanders. I didn't hear anything about that. I tried to get out of their way. I stuck with my unit, my other co-troops in my unit and nobody of the locals wanted to have anything to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now did there come to be a time-period when you were assigned to some other village, other than Prelovo as part of your fulfilment of you military service duties, upon mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, just Rujiste, while I was -- until the 1st of June, 1993. After that I was sent to Kladanj, Niksicka, Visoravan, Jabuka, around Gorazde, to man the front line. This is where I was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off, I believe, talking about the White Eagles. I have just one more -- or a couple of more questions on that before moving on to my remaining topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, if we can call up P229 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A photograph will be shown to you in a moment, sir. And if can we can zoom in on the part of the Exhibit that's a photograph. Thank you. Do you recognise either of these two individuals depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has testified that he has trouble with his eyesight perhaps we can established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The witness has testified that he has trouble with his eyesight. Perhaps it might be an idea to establish how well can he or cannot see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did volunteer that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's back up a bit. Can you describe for us what you see depicted in this photograph. I'm sorry, sir, [Previous translation continues] ... didn't get to you. Can you describe for us what you visually see in this photograph. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I can see these people here with a vehicle, and I see this writing with Faith in God. I see automatic rifles in their hands. That's what I can see. The car, I don't know which make ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, based upon what you can see, do you see enough to recognise either of these two individuals that are depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: You want me to tell you who they are. On the left side, is Stevo Milosavljevic, and on the right-hand side is Josip Stevanovic. He worked with me from 1989 to 1992 in maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the first part of your answer, right and left from what perspective? From what perspective right and left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: As they are looking at me, on the left is Stevo Milosavljevic. On the right-hand side is Josip Stevanovic. He worked with me in Varda in maintenance in the same workshop. They were locksmiths, and one of them was a driver, and I was one of the sharpeners.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these individuals now, were either one of them known, reputed, or otherwise believed to be members of the White Eagles or of any paramilitary organisation in Visegrad in 1992, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Both of them -- I mean, neither of them were white eagles or in paramilitary units. They drove food supplies to troops at Poceva [phoen] in Kabernik [phoen]. They only drove food supplies, because Josip was an invalid and he was not an able-bodied man. He could in the be involved in combat or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the head gear on the man on the left? What can you tell us about that head gear. What kind of hat is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: It looks like the so-called Tito`s cap. I'm not sure if it is a fur cap. It has the eagle sign on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the gentleman on the right? What kind of head gear does he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: That is a sajkaca known as the Serbian peasant hat. Half the world wears caps like that. Even I wore one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now moving on to the other area you mentioned just before the break that you had been stationed in Rujiste at some point in time. Could you briefly tell us where the army was stationed in Rujiste vis-a-vis the village itself or the roadway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Overlooking the village closer to Kamenica which is a Muslim village, and also facing Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Zenica is a Muslim village; and Kamenica is mainly a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There seems to be some confusion. I guess the best way for me to resolve this is to ask you, sir, with respect to Kamenica, what ethnicity predominantly lives in Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Muslim. Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that region or that locale, where were the enemy front lines of the Muslim forces situated in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: There were no Muslim forces except across the Drina river towards Zepa. On our side there were no Muslim forces on that location overlooking Rujiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about the civilian population of Rujiste, where were they located or situated? Where did they spend their nights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Left from our line that we were holding, about 800 metres to the left. And all the civilians, and I know them all by name, slept close to our tents, because they did not dare move too far away from us, because Zepa was close, just across the Drina river.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say they did not dare to move too far away from us, why was that? Why couldn't they go and reside in their own village, in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: They didn't dare to. They were Siptars [as interpreted] there, and it was a Muslim village, and there were army troops close to Rujiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any neighbouring villages that had been adversely affected or destroyed in 1992 by the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, there was Sitarevo and Kamenica and Zenica, but I don't know what army damaged or destroyed them. When we came on the 22nd of May, we just stood guard there. We just held our own line. I mean, our company did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can try to correct -- correct something that has come up in the translation at page 41, line 10, your answer is recorded as, "they didn't dare to. They were Siptars there. And it was a Muslim village." Is that in fact what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, no, no. It is not "Siptars." It's the village called "Sitarevo" a Muslim village, a Muslim village called Sitarevo. It was misunderstood or maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was this village one of the villages that was destroyed in the course of fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: The village was not completely destroyed. There were some houses and barns remaining standing. It wasn't destroyed when we came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to run into or encounter the parents of Milan Lukic whilst stopped in Rujiste with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes. I did pass by their tent on the 13th of June when I was going home to have a bath, together with another three or four soldiers. We ran into his parents. They were both in tears. I asked, Why are you crying? And they said there was action up there, in Kopito. He might have gotten killed. I said go and see the commander. He will tell you. And when I came home, my wife said, Milorad, three men died in Gornja Lijeska, Commander Trifkovic who was battalion commander got killed. Vlatko Filipovic, and another man Veljko got killed. I don't know if they had any connections, but eventually I found out that he wasn't killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's try and -- so I'm going to have to try and break it up so to make it easier to understand. First of all, what was your schedule like in the army that was stationed up in Rujiste in terms of when you be on service and when you would leave or a break?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: It was in seven-day stints or even 15-day stints when they were not enough troops. And when we went home on leave we would stay for two or three days. And later on, when there was action at Kopita, we had just one night go back home to change to have a bath, and then we had to go back immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and with respect to your encounter with the parents of Milan Lukic, why did they believe that their son might have been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Because he was up there on the line, on Simic Kopita. The road was cut off on the 13th. They could not go back until the 15th of June. The road was only opened on the 15th. That's why they were crying. They thought that they might have gotten killed. It is terrible for parents in war whenever they hear about someone getting killed, they think it could be their child.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what news or event had occurred on the 13th that had gotten back to the people in Visegrad that led them to think that Milan had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Only his parents thought that. Because every parent thinks the worst when they hear of even an accident. But, fortunately, it was not Milan. It was Trifkovic and Novica, Savic and Veljko Mirkovic who got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say that when you ... you say you came home and then talked with your wife and discovered that Trifkovic and these others that had been killed. Let me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you how long did you remain at your home before returning to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We need a redaction for that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen at your home that next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, the Orthodox Trinity holiday. I was waiting for the van to take me to the line in Rujiste. A group of Muslims came by. They came to the gate. They were all standing there --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down and tell the names more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... private session, just to air on the side of caution since he is speaking so fast. I'm not sure exactly everything that he is going to say. He might mention details that would identify him or other protected persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, just for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, again if you could listen to the Judge`s instruction and please speak very slowly when describing every detail of this. Could you tell us -- repeat your answer to my question which was: Did anything unusual happen at your home that next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: On the 14th, it was a Sunday, it was the Orthodox Trinity holiday. I was at home sitting there. A group of Kortik [as interpreted] came. I didn't know where they were going until they came up to me and told me, Would you go with us to Sase. A bus is waiting for to us to go Kladanj. I said, please, don't take me. I have to stay here. I am waiting for a van to go to the line in Rujiste. I can't miss the van. And they said, Please, by God, if you come with us, if we run into some troops, nobody will touch us, nobody will dare if you are with us. And I told them, I will go with you, but if I see a van taking troops to the front line, I will have to go with it. I went with them. I went all the way to Sase. We found that bus that had come to take them. It was broken down. It got stuck in a canal. The driver went out to look for a new vehicle. I sat with them, and I saw that finally the time is coming up when the van was going to pick up with them. There was a house nearby. I went out and asked a lady to call 92, the SUP, and to ask them when the bus would come to pick up those people. She called, and they answered, Let them wait. The bus will come. I continued to sit with them and wait. But there was no bus. The lady told me the SUP people had called again, and said, The commander gave them a message to go walk to town. A bus would come and take them Kladanj, and then my van came, and I got into it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we request that prior session all be retroactively made in open session as nothing has been revealed whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. That's fine. That's fine. This next question, though, might. Let me just ask, and then we can find out and retroactively put it in open if it does not reveal anything that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When had you first started answering the question, you had mentioned some names. Could you tell us specifically who from this Koritnik group you encountered, and in particular, anyone that entered into your home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: They came to my yard, and I went with them into Sase. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who are these persons from Koritnik that came into your yard? Could you name them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I can only tell you the names of people who were there, and there were five, maybe six, women who were there. There was some younger people whom I didn't know. I know them only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you had indicated that someone had asked to you accompany them. Who specifically asked you and begged you to accompany them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Esma Kurspahic and her son Mirza, they came into my yard and they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I think we can go back into open session from this point on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This group from Koritnik that you have identified, about how many persons were there in this group that you could see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Not more than 30, 32. Certainly not more. I know every man by name. Every person by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see them all with your own eyes, all the persons that there were on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: They were all standing next to me on the road but my gate. I went with them to Sase all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to take the opportunity to ask you about certain persons, whether they were there in that group and what can you tell us about them. First of all, I'd like to ask you about Ajanovic Mule who in 1992 would have been approximately 75 years of age. Was this individual in that group from Koritnik that came down the road that you encountered that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about three individuals with the last name Delija and the first names Adis, 2 years of age; Ajnija, 50 years of age; and Jasmina, approximately 24 years of age. Were those persons in that group that you saw and spoke with on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: They were not there at all. They were across the Drina. The houses were across the Drina, and they were closer to Rogatica, if you went to the woods, then to the town of Visegrad. There was no need for them to come to our way to go to Sase because all -- we were all Serbs on this side, and on the other side there were all Muslims. I told at the beginning all the last names, and there was one Kada Sejic, born in Koritnik. She went with her son Faruk. And she spent the night in Koritnik and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, again, you're speaking very fast. If you could slow down and please let me go through my list, it will be much easier for us all to understand everything you have to testify about if you allow me to break it down into pieces. Now, for -- we left off, I believe, if I can ask you about Jasarevic, Tima; Jasarevic, Hajra; Jasarevic, Meho; and Jasarevic, Mujo. Were any of those persons there in that group from Koritnik on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Those people were not from Koritnik at all. They were closer to Sase. There were none of them there. Mujo Jasarevic was an elderly man. He had died about ten years before the war. I attended his funeral I used to work him, and we knew each other. I don't know who told you that he was there. You can't believe that list. There was not a single Jasarevic. And Jatina [phoen], what's her name, wasn't there. No one with that last name was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You have already identified for us that Mujo died ten years before the start of the war. What can you tell us about Hajda Jasarevic. Do you have any knowledge as to Hajda Jasarevic, where that person resides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that name at all. I didn't see that woman at all. There was no one from the Jasarevics.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to -- let's go through now -- Aisa Kurspahic, approximately 49 years old in 1992. Was that individual part of the group that was from Koritnik that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: As far as I remember, she was there. She might been Redzo's wife or Becar's, or Jasen's, but she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Aida Kurspahic, 12 years old, approximately. Was that individual there in that group on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Was no one 12 years old. There was only one Faruk Sejic. There was no one younger. And there was a very, very small baby, maybe two days old, in the arms of his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Aika Kurspahic, 62 years ago old, was that individual there on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Alija Kurspahic, 55 years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, Alija was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Almir Kurspahic, approximately 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of an Almir Kurspahic who would have been ten years old existing in Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Never heard. Never heard. Maybe he existed, but he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Aner Kurspahic, approximately six years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: How old?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Six years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Betsar [phoen] -- or Becar Kurspahic, approximately 52 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Becar Kurspahic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about a lady approximately 50 years of age, Bisera Kurspahic. Was she is was she part of that group that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that name. It's not familiar. Even if she was there, I wouldn't have known her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about a Bula Kurspahic, approximately 58.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, Bula was there. She was Ismet Kurspahic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by the way, is Bula her real name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. No. She must have another real name, but Bula is the name given to women who prepare a dead woman's body for the rites.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Dzheva Kurspahic, approximately 22 years of age.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, she wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Enesa Kurspahic, two years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. Not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Hasa Kurspahic, 18 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, she wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Hajrija Kurspahic, 60 years old. Was she in that group that you had seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, she was there. I know the older people, and I'm sure that she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Halida Kurspahic, 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, she wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Apart from those you have already identified, I believe you identified Faruk as being a young baby and the Mirza as being a teenager. Were there any other children in that group? If not, I can skip them on this reading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, there were no other children apart from the two day -- the baby of two days, Faruk of 12 years, and Mirza who was 14. He said that he was 14 when he came to my house. But no other younger people, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me skip ahead then to some who are older age. What about Hasnija Kurspahic, aged 62? Was that individual there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Hata Kurspahic, 68 years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: She was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... about Hata Kurspahic and your observations with respect to her on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. I didn't observe anything. They all behaved in the same way. She didn't stick out from the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Ifeta Kurspahic, 17 years old.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, she wasn't there. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Kurspahic Igabala. Was she there, aged 58?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Igabala Kurspahic, I don't know the name. But if I may say, they were all older people. They were two younger girls. One was Esena, and I don't know the name of the other. And the women who were there were the wives of the men. Now I know all the men by name. And there were four women, Mula Ajanovic, Bula who -- the widow of Ismet who worked in Austria, and there was Hajda, and there was Kada. And the -- the Sejic woman. These were the only women without husbands there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Ismeta Kurspahic, who would have been about 26? What can you tell us about that person? First of all, did you see her on the 14th of June 1992 with that group from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. I'm sure she was not there. I'm quite certain. If I -- if she had been there, I would have told you so. But she wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What else can you tell us about her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: In 1994, when we're up at Jabuka, there was a mountain by the name of Bula, and they had a tent there in which they cooked, and on a tree I saw the inscription Ismet Kurspahic and Hasena Kurspahic. So I saw the names on the tree. They were probably cooks who worked there in the tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you say they had a tent there. Who is it that had this tent there that you found in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Well, it was a Muslim tent, and I know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it a civilian tent or a military tent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: There was a kitchen there. We saw food and the other stuff, so it was clear that they had their kitchen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Kada Kurspahic, aged 40? Was she on that -- was she there with that group on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I never even heard of that Kada Kurspahic. And I really spent many years there. There was only Kada Sejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What -- what about Latifa Kurspahic who would have been approximately 23 years of age? Was she part of that group from Koritnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm -- I'm not familiar with the name. There were three or four younger girls. That's all. I don't know them all by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Medina Kurspahic? Was she there, in that group that you saw on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I know that person. She was the daughter of Medo Kurspahic, and she had a sister at a -- at a kindergarten near the village. She was not part of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Medo Kurspahic. Was Medo Kurspahic, aged 50, there, in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Meira Kurspahic, aged 47, was that individual in that group that you saw op that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that name, and I'm sure she wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Meva Kurspahic, aged 45.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, she wasn't there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Mujesera Kurspahic, age 35. Or Mujesera is a perhaps a better pronunciation. Aged 35?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, there was no one of that age there. I'm certain of that. The same sounds somewhat familiar, but she wasn't there. I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Munivera Kurspahic, aged 20?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that one. She wasn't there, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Munira Kurspahic, aged 55?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: She was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Osman Kurspahic, aged 67? Was that individual part of the group that you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure, Osman was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Hasijar Pasija Kurspahic, aged 56?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Pasija Kurspahic the wife the Edem, she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Ramiza Kurspahic, aged 57?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't remember that name at all. I don't know if she was there. Actually she certainly wasn't there. I would have known the older women by name, but I don't remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Kurspahic, Safa, aged 50, was that individual in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't remember her either. She can't have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Kurspahic Saha, aged 70? Aged 70.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: She was there. She was a big fat women; I remember her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Kurspahic Sumbula, aged 62? Was that individual there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, she was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm skipping ahead, skip any minors. What about Memisevic Fazila, was that individual a part of the group you encountered form Koritnik on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: There were only two Memisevics, Redzo and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about Sadikovic Rabija, 52 years of age, was that individual there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: There was no such women was there. The last name Sadikovic cannot be found there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have -- you've already mentioned Sejic Kada. What about Velic, Nurka? Was that individual present in that group that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Nurka Velic, she is from another village. She wasn't there. Kada Sejic was there, because she was the daughter of Asip [phoen] Kurspahic and she was with her -- at her father's house, and that's why she was part of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Velic, Tima, who would have been 35 years of age. Was that individual part of that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No that is Mirka's daughter, the same, Mirka [phoen] Velic. She is was from another village, and she wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have as knowledge as to Tima Velic, as to where that individual lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know why they went. I heard from people in the townsfolk that she is alive, but I don't where she lives. She must have left before the war or in the early days of the war, but I heard people saying that she was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who is Timke Velic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I don't know that person at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Timke Velic, T-i-m-k-e?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No, I don't know that person at all. And she wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And lastly, what about Jasmina Vila, was any individual by that name part of that group that you saw from Koritnik on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. She wasn't there. She was from another village, Musici toward Prelovo, but it is a long village. Toward Kortalic [phoen]. I said at the beginning that there were only four last names, Kurspahic, Ajanovic, Redzo Memisevic, and Kada Sejic. That's all. And those were all the family names that could be found there in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness in direct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just before you begin, Ms. Marcus, for the purposes of the record, and the court deputy, the pages that are to be placed in public session, page 44, line 13 to page 45, line 18. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, I hate to be clerk-like here. But tomorrow they will be assigned completely different numbers. Perhaps, Your Honour, can say the first sentence and last independence, we will be able to find that tomorrow when it is repaginated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the transcript. It will be done. Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before we begin, I just wanted to put on the record the fact that this witness had been given a pseudonym, another pseudonym, in early filings relating to the alibi. We discussed that briefly during the break, and perhaps, just to call the Chamber's attention to that, I think at some point for it to be clarified on the record that those two pseudonyms refer to the same person. I think -- he wasn't granted protective measures, but the earlier filings used a pseudonym because he was in an order of pseudonyms that the Defence was, I suppose, anticipating might be used for this witness. And because some of the litigation as to this case refers to him under that pseudonym, just to avoid any confusion, it might be an idea at some point to put on the record that the two pseudonyms refer to the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: And what is the other pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: MLD 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just -- you're satisfied with that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, although at that time no protective measures were sought for MLD 6. It was a proposed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [previous translation continues] ... refer to the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I can verify that that is, I believe, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness has given approximately 12 pages of evidence in relation to the Pionirska Street fire, in fact, I have actually 19 pages of evidence in relation to the events of Pionirska Street and the victims of the Pionirska fire, and as far as I have approximately one page in relation to the alibi at Kopito. So I would just like to request of the Chamber - I will do my very best in terms of cross-examination - but we would like to request that the Chamber ask the witness to stay back, and by tomorrow afternoon we will left the Chamber know whether there is any further cross-examination on this brand new evidence that was completely unnoticed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, although again I stress that the statement disclosed to us by the Office of the Prosecutor talks precisely about this event that they had no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I will ask that witness remain behind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, my name is Maxine Marcus, and I will be asking awe few questions today on behalf of the Prosecution. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, before the question, could I please request private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: MLD 24, under the Republika Srpska Criminal Code misleading a competent body into certifying a false matter in a public document, register, or book could constitute a violation punishable by law with imprisonment of up to two years. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Under the same Republika Srpska Criminal Code creating a false document or altering a genuine document could similarly constitute a violation punishable by law with imprisonment of up to three years. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And finally, under that same code, creating a false document or altering a genuine public document and putting it into circulation or keeping it in order to use it or, in fact, using it could be a violation punishable with up to five years of imprisonment, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: MLD 24 you were a member of the army of Republika Srpska as you have testified. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And your dates of service, I believe, you said, were from the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992, until the 1st of July, 1993. I was in the regular army, and after that I was under work duty as I stated in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify, your service lasted until the 1st of July 1993 or the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: The 1st of July. I have a document listing all my positions where I was on duty, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you did engage in military operations after that time during the war all the way through 1995, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Until the 30th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What unit did you operate in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: I was in a company, Rujiste Company. There is a military post number, but I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Slavko Vojnovic until the 1st of July 1993, he was a company commander. After that we did not have any commander. Whenever a courier would come to home and said reports to this or this place at Okoliste, and then among soldiers we would be pointed to go to different positions to replace the people manning the front line, and this is how we did and they did. We had no commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, throughout your military service, would you agree that there was active armed combat in Visegrad and the surrounding municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, there was in the surrounding municipalities at Medjedja, Gorazde, Rogatica, but I don't go there. The furthest I went in the direction of the Gorazde was Jabuka.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And during that time there was armed combat within Visegrad municipality as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: No. From the 1st of July there were no conflicts in Visegrad. Well, the only places where there was some action was at Sjemec and around Kopita and that sort of places.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now in the months of May and June of 1992, there were hostilities in Visegrad municipality. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD24
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Yes, there was on that other side by -- on the part of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
